- If sentiment shows strong bullish (e.g., 1.00) in recent days, model tends to over-forecast; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment shows strong bearish (e.g., -1.00), model often under-forecasts; adjust downward bias or increase sensitivity to recent lows.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast growth rate by 20–30% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (e.g., 0.00 or 0.25), model often drifts toward mean reversion — forecast should be anchored to recent 7–14 day average, not extrapolated trend.
- If true outcome shows strong divergence from forecast in early days (e.g., first 5–7 days), sentiment may be misaligned — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment shift within 2–3 days of data update.
- Model tends to overestimate volatility in high-sentiment periods — reduce forecast variance by 15–20% when sentiment > 0.50.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., price drops after spike), model often fails to recognize — apply “reversion buffer”: if price > 1.5x recent high, cap forecast at 1.2x high for 3–5 days.
